cues.text: Section six is a model essay.
A model essay shows you how to structure a strong answer to an exam-style question, so we will work through the question and then the points a good answer should cover, in order.
The question is this: secure a campus wireless and wired network.
The task is to design and justify a security approach for one campus network that has both Wi-Fi and cabled connections.
The question begins by asking you to explain four risks: shared radio, rogue APs, credential compromise and lateral movement.
The first risk is shared radio.
Wireless traffic travels through the air, and anyone within range can receive the signal.
A cable gives a physical point of access, but a radio signal does not stop at the wall of a lecture hall.
That is why wireless needs strong authentication and encryption.
The second risk is rogue APs.
An AP is an access point, the device that connects wireless clients to the network.
A rogue AP is one that has not been authorised by the organisation.
It might be a device someone plugs in for convenience, or one set up deliberately to attract users and capture their traffic.
The third risk is credential compromise.
If an attacker obtains a valid username and password, the network may treat them as a legitimate user.
The fourth risk is lateral movement.
After gaining a foothold on one device or account, an attacker moves sideways from system to system inside the network.
A flat network with no internal barriers makes this much easier.
Next come the controls, and the question asks you to choose them in a justified way.
First, choose appropriate 802.11 bands after site survey.
802.11 is the IEEE standard family for wireless LANs.
A site survey examines the actual building: coverage, interference, and where access points should go.
The band choice should follow that evidence rather than assumption.
Second, use WPA3-Enterprise with 802.1X, with certificate validation where supported.
WPA3-Enterprise is the enterprise-grade wireless security mode, in which each user is authenticated individually rather than everyone sharing one password.
802.1X is the port-based network access control standard that makes this possible.
Certificate validation means the client checks the identity certificate of the authentication server.
This helps protect users from connecting to a rogue AP that is impersonating the real network.
The qualification matters: do this where supported, because some devices cannot do it.
Third, separate guest and staff/student VLANs.
A VLAN, or virtual LAN, divides one physical network into separate logical networks.
Guests then cannot directly reach internal staff and student resources, and this limits lateral movement.
Fourth, use role-based access.
What a person can reach depends on their role, for example staff, student or guest, rather than on everyone receiving the same access.
Fifth, apply firewall and ACL policy.
ACL stands for access control list, a set of rules that permits or denies traffic.
Together, firewalls and ACLs enforce which networks and services may talk to which.
Sixth, secure management.
The tools used to administer switches, access points and servers must themselves be protected, because anyone who controls them controls the network.
Seventh, provide a monitored VPN for remote access.
A VPN, or virtual private network, creates a protected tunnel for users who connect from outside the campus.
The word monitored is part of the requirement: remote access should be logged and watched, not simply allowed.
The essay then makes a point about two further protections.
TLS authenticates endpoints via PKI and encrypts application traffic.
TLS is Transport Layer Security.
PKI is public key infrastructure, the system of certificates and trusted authorities that lets one party verify who the other party really is.
So TLS lets a client confirm it is talking to the genuine server, and it encrypts the application data in transit.
The source also says MFA complements rather than replaces it.
MFA is multi-factor authentication, which requires more than one kind of proof of identity.
It adds protection for the user's login, but it does not do TLS's job of authenticating endpoints and encrypting traffic, so the two work together.
The answer should also include IDS and IPS, patching, logs, backups and tested recovery.
An IDS, an intrusion detection system, detects suspicious activity.
An IPS, an intrusion prevention system, can also act to block it.
Patching fixes known vulnerabilities in software and devices.
Logs record events so that incidents can be investigated.
Backups give you a copy of data, and tested recovery means you have actually checked that you can restore from them, rather than just assuming that you can.
The question also asks you to justify trade-offs for compatibility, cost and usability.
A strong answer does not simply list controls.
It explains why they were chosen and what they cost.
Compatibility matters because some devices may not support every feature, which is why the certificate validation requirement is qualified with where supported.
Cost matters because security must fit a budget.
Usability matters because controls that are too hard to use push people to work around them.
Finally, the answer should show how Zero Trust continuously limits access rather than trusting all internal clients.
In Zero Trust, being inside the campus network does not make a device or user trustworthy.
Access is limited and checked continuously.
This links back to the earlier risks: if an attacker compromises one credential or one device, Zero Trust restricts how far they can go.
